reason: The court made a fact-specific preference for the notary and attesting witness evidence in this case, not a general rule that their presence indicates deed authenticity.
The court held section 31 non-compliance did not invalidate the deed, but the statement omits section 33's limitation to matters of form and its proviso for other written law.
The court held that the observed abnormal conduct, without medical evidence, did not prove Alice de Silva was deranged or insane when executing the deed.
The quoted voidable-contract formulation is from Soysa v Soysa and was not the specific holding of this appeal on Alice de Silva's capacity.
The court applied the delusions principle to reject incapacity, but the supporting wording is a quotation from Soysa v Soysa rather than this court's own statement.
The court held that the non-notarial agreement to sell land contravened section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and was invalid.
The court treated a notice to quit as a condition precedent to the landlord's successful ejectment action.
The court expressly held that a contract of tenancy in this case had to be proved on a balance of probability.
The court held that a pure question of law not dependent on facts may be decided before judgment even without an issue or evidence.
The concession about receipt of the section 32(4) notice was merely a pleaded fact in this case, not a legal holding.
The rule was about the 30-day action period after notice under section 32(4) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, which the statement omits.
The court held heirs of the donee had only a contingent interest, but only in the context of a revocable Kandyan gift whose revocation right had not been renounced.
The court recognised the donor's lifetime right of revocation, but the statement omits the statutory exceptions and the need that the right of revocation not have been renounced.
The minor-transfer rule was decided under Roman-Dutch-law authorities, while SRC051-s10(1) is only the Land Acquisition Act reference mechanism used to bring the title dispute to court.
The need for the minor transferor to seek restitutio-in-integrum was the holding, but Land Acquisition Act s10(1) was not the provision construed for that rule.
The maxim was explanatory support for the minor's need to seek court relief, not the case's operative rule, and the cited Land Acquisition Act section was not construed for it.
The source of Enso Nona's marriage certificate was a preliminary factual premise, not the legal holding on succession.
The court recited section 3(2), but the operative holding was that the marriage was presumed Diga and Enso Nona therefore did not inherit from her father.
The Diga presumption was applied, but the statement omits that it applies to a person governed by Kandyan law and is rebuttable by contrary proof.

The court required proof that the plaintiff paid or provided the consideration despite transfer in the defendant's name, not the vague proposition that consideration is independent of the transferee's name.
The court treated intention as a separate section 84 element and said it was irrelevant once the plaintiff failed to prove payment or provision of consideration.
The court adopted the practice allowing even an intervenient to prove title to an unallotted share after interlocutory decree and remitted the application for inquiry.
The court recognised a party's right to prove title to a share left unallotted in the final decree and set aside the refusal to inquire into that claim.
The court's holding was confined to partition proceedings where section 48(4) could not cure non-issue of summons or lack of jurisdiction, which the statement omits.
The quoted language supported relief from an unlawfully obtained partition decree, but the statement is too vague to state the actual procedural holding.
